title: Accessibility Check Walkthrough
creator: Dan McCreary
subject: Accessibility
WCAG
Keyboard Operability
Universal Design for Learning
MicroSim Quality Review
description: A p5.js MicroSim in which learners run four human accessibility checks (keyboard-only completion, visible focus, text alternative and no color-only meaning) on three variants of a mock ball-drop MicroSim, record Pass or Fail verdicts, and compare them with the built-in defects, each mismatch explained in one sentence.
audience: Teachers, instructional designers, learning-technology developers and learning-analytics practitioners (college undergraduate and professional development)

learningObjectives: The learner will judge whether a mock MicroSim passes each of four accessibility checks and justify each verdict with the defect they found.
prerequisites: Accessibility standards, keyboard operability and the accessibility check (Chapter 24)
Operating a web page with Tab, Shift+Tab, arrow keys and Enter
standards: WCAG 2.1 AA: 1.1.1 Non-text Content, 1.4.1 Use of Color, 2.1.1 Keyboard, 2.4.7 Focus Visible

accessibility.notes: All controls are native labeled elements with a 3px focus ring; the mock is operable from the keyboard while the canvas has focus and never traps focus; verdicts are shown as words and symbols as well as colors; reveal results are announced in an aria-live region; describe() text is updated after every change

controls.label: Mock variant
controls.purpose: Choose mock variant A, B or C

controls.label: Keyboard only
controls.purpose: Disable pointer input on the mock so the task must be done with Tab, arrow keys and Enter

controls.label: Show description
controls.purpose: Hide the mock picture and show the text a screen reader would read

controls.label: Keyboard / Focus / Text alt / Color
controls.purpose: Record a Pass or Fail verdict for each of the four checks

controls.label: Reveal answers
controls.purpose: Compare verdicts with the built-in defects and explain each mismatch

simulation.model: Mock MicroSim with built-in, deliberate accessibility defects (not real product findings)
assumptions: Variant A: pointer-only canvas slider and a vague description
Variant B: hidden focus indicator and a status light that relies on red versus green
Variant C: passes all four checks

pedagogical.teachingStrategy: Hands-on evaluation against a checklist, followed by feedback on each verdict
pedagogical.interactionPattern: Operate a mock, record verdicts, reveal and compare
keyQuestions: Can every function be reached and used from the keyboard?
Can you always see where keyboard focus is?
Does the text alternative alone tell a listener what is shown and what the controls do?
Is any information carried only by color?
commonMisconceptions: If a control can be focused, focus is visible
Any describe() text satisfies the text alternative check
Automated tools can run all four checks
assessmentOpportunities: Verdicts that match the built-in answers
A written defect for each Fail verdict
A minimal repair plan for each defect
